items.q: An ad server stores ads and decides which one to show.
items.why: It holds the creatives and chooses between campaigns each time an ad is requested.

items.q: A publisher ad server and an advertiser ad server do exactly the same job.
items.why: The publisher side manages inventory. The advertiser side tracks campaigns across many sites.

items.q: A line item holds a campaign’s delivery instructions inside an ad server.
items.why: Dates, targeting, priority and budget are set on the line item.

items.q: Ad servers can count impressions and clicks.
items.why: That counting is the basis for delivery and billing reports.

items.q: Priority settings help decide which line item wins when several could serve.
items.why: Higher priority line items are considered first.

items.q: A creative is the actual ad file or code that appears on the page.
items.why: It can be an image, a video or interactive code.

items.q: An ad tag is a small piece of code that asks the ad server for an ad.
items.why: The page runs the tag, and the server answers with a creative.

items.q: Frequency capping can only be handled by the browser.
items.why: Ad servers and buying platforms usually enforce it using IDs and counts.

items.q: A third-party tag lets an advertiser’s own ad server deliver the creative through the publisher’s ad server.
items.why: The publisher server hands the call on, so the advertiser can count independently.

items.q: Pacing in an ad server can spread a campaign’s impressions across its dates.
items.why: Even pacing avoids using the whole budget on the first day.
